text: You get a sorted array that was rotated at some unknown point. This time it's sorted non-decreasing, so it may contain duplicates. Return true if the target is in there, false otherwise. And afterwards I'll ask you whether the duplicates change the complexity.
Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — I only return a boolean here, not an index. Is that right?

Good. Let me say the hard part out loud, because the duplicates break something specific. Without duplicates, the search rests on one fact: rotating makes exactly one break point, so if I cut at the middle, the other half is fully sorted. That fact is still true here. What breaks is detecting which half is sorted. I detect it by comparing nums at left against nums at mid. With duplicates those two can be equal, and then two different situations look identical: the left half might be one flat run, or it might straddle the break and just start and end on the same value. Comparing them tells me nothing.

Here's the smallest case that shows the damage: zero, one, zero, zero, zero, looking for one. Middle is index two, and both ends of the left half are zero. A plain sorted-half test reads that as left half sorted, with range zero to zero, decides one isn't in there, and throws the whole left side away. But the left side is zero, one, zero — not sorted at all, and the answer was sitting in it.
Are there any constraints on the input size?
Up to five thousand elements, values within ten thousand either way.

Let me run through the example: two, five, six, zero, zero, one, two, target zero. Note the head and the tail are both two, so this input can hit the ambiguous case. The answer is true — there are two zeros, at indices three and four.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to scan the whole array. It's linear time, and — I'll come back to this — that turns out to match the worst case of anything I can write. But it gives up on every easy input. This problem reminds me of modified binary search on a rotated array — keep the half that's provably sorted — plus a fallback for when I can't tell the direction. When comparing tells me nothing, I stop trying to halve and just give up one cell. So: halve when I can, shrink by one when I must.

Here's the plan. One: keep a closed range and shrink it to one cell. Two: if nums at left equals nums at mid, check that cell against the target, then drop it. Three: otherwise, keep the side the target can be in, and check the last cell. One thing worth flagging — the check before dropping the cell is the whole ballgame. Every other shrink comes with a proof that the target can't be there; this one is a blind discard. The only way to discard blindly and stay correct is to look at the cell first. And the direction isn't free: I checked nums at left, not nums at right, so moving right down would discard a cell I never looked at. There's a trade-off here: the fallback costs the log-time guarantee. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. First comes the new branch: if nums at left equals nums at mid, I return true if that cell is the target, otherwise move left up by one and continue. After that, it's the usual sorted-half logic — move into the sorted half if the target is inside its range, else jump to the other side. At the end I return whether the one remaining cell equals the target. One thing worth flagging — the sortedness test here is a strict less-than. Without duplicates it has to be less-or-equal, because with two cells left, mid equals left. Here the equal case is already caught above, so an equals sign would be dead code — strict less-than says exactly what it guards.

Let's dry-run the code: two, five, six, zero, zero, one, two, target zero, expected true. The third row is the new case: both ends read six, so I learn nothing and give up one cell — but only after confirming that six isn't the target. The loop then ends at index three, and nums at three is zero, so I return true. Corner cases: one, zero, one, one, one, looking for zero, is found inside the equal branch — delete that check and it returns false. A single cell never enters the loop. All ones, looking for two, is the worst shape — one cell per round. A cross-check against a linear scan on over half a million cases found no disagreements.

Now your follow-up. Yes, duplicates change the complexity, and they change the class, not the constant. The time complexity is log n when the ends differ, but linear in the worst case. The space complexity is constant. I measured it: at five thousand elements, the worst input takes four thousand nine hundred ninety-nine passes, exactly n minus one, while a duplicate-free array of the same size takes thirteen. In the worst-case scenario the array is all equal with the target absent, so every round learns nothing and gives up one cell. Oh, one more thing — linear isn't a weakness of this solution, it's a lower bound on the problem. Picture five thousand ones with a single zero hidden somewhere. Unseen cells are indistinguishable from outside, so an adversary puts the zero where you didn't look. Any algorithm must read linear cells in the worst case.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You separated the invariant from the way you detect it — the at-least-one-half-is-sorted fact survives, only the comparison stops working — and you showed the exact input where the old logic throws the answer away. You explained the blind discard as needing its own check, and caught that moving right down would discard a cell you never examined. And you answered the complexity follow-up with measured numbers, then argued the linear bound is the problem's, not yours. Good work.
